newsitem.title: SPAIN: Investors to favour short Spanish bonds over peseta.
newsitem.headline: Investors to favour short Spanish bonds over peseta.

text.p: Spain's sleepy peseta has little to offer in the run-up to Europe's economic and monetary union and funds searching for good returns should head instead for the short-end of the Spanish bond market, analysts said on Thursday.
As Spain steams along the road to EMU, analysts agree the peseta will remain at the mercy of the central bank and is unlikely to break out of a band from 84 to 85 per mark well into next year.
Five analysts interviewed by Reuters believed that if EMU goes ahead, the currency would probably enter at a rate based on its central parity at around 85.07 to 85.25, leaving little room for profit.

"The currency is set to lose around 0.8 percent over the next one-and-half years and the bond market offers more interest as Spain must lower rates if they are to be one of the first members of EMU," said Ralf Schreyer, a director and investor for DWG in Frankfurt.
While peseta investors agreed rates must go lower into next year, they differed on how much and the exact part of the curve where they would focus funds.

But most were united in the belief that the long-end of the curve holds little value after a strong rally since the beginning of 1996 and the last morsels of profit are to be found in the short-end ahead of convergence.
Bank of America economist Henrik Lumholdt sees the Bank of Spain's key money market rate falling 50 basis points to 4.75 percent this year and a further 25 to 50 bps next year.
His ideal investment would go no further out than two years on the curve. More specifically he targeted the 8.30 percent December 1998 bond or 9.40 percent April 1999.

"Here you are almost entirely hedged against possible turmoil in the process toward EMU and against the scenario that the whole thing would have to be called off and the Bank of Spain would tighten its belt," Lumholdt said.
Schreyer was more radical.
"We expect money market rates at the end of this year at something close to four percent and frankly the market has not priced in such a substantial fall," he said.
Based on this, Schreyer believes a structured deal based on short rates with no currency view would be the best bet.

"The money market rates, Libor strips and two-years, are not pricing in enough lowering. I would like to structure something like a bet on 6-months or even one-year...this would offer good value," he said.

Societe Generale's chief economist Alfredo Urrutia believes interest rates will break five percent by year-end, and sees most value in the three to five-year area of the curve, providing the best risk-reward if Spain does converge.

"Unless the Bank of Spain can find an enhanced margin for cutting rates, I think the very short-end of the Spanish bond market has priced in quite an aggressive position and most of the margin has been eaten up," Urrutia said.

As a rough guide of how far the market expects interest rates to fall this year, the Mibor futures September contract was trading on Thursday around a yield of 4.97, while the December contract hovered near 4.91.

"This is tantamount to saying that the market is discounting a 25 basis point cut by year-end. Even if you look at contracts further out into next year, the market is only discounting one move down to 5.00 percent or a little bit less," Lumholdt said.
"The market thinks there is just one shot left in the gun and in my view they are underestimating the amount of monetary easing," he added.

The Bank of Spain has slashed its key money market rate from a level of 9.25 percent at the end of 1995 to a current rate of 5.25 percent helping to fuel a dramatic rally in Spanish bonds. Germany's repo rate currently stands at three percent.
The yield spread between Spanish and German 10-year benchmark bonds has fallen from 330 bps in March 1996 to a current level of 70 bps.
